opus-5.5.text:
I think the ideal is that it feels less like using a bunch of separate tools and more like working with one really capable collaborator. Right now you have this fragmentation: you go to one place to do deep research, another place for something that can take actions in a browser, another for coding, and you're kind of the router, deciding which product to use for which task. I don't think users should have to do that. You should just be able to say what you want, and the system figures out whether it needs to search, go off and browse, write and run some code, or just answer you directly.

The other big piece is that it should feel really natural to move between synchronous and asynchronous work. Sometimes you want a quick back-and-forth, and sometimes you want to hand something off, have the agent work on it for twenty minutes or a few hours, and come back to you when it's done or when it actually needs your input. So the interface needs to support delegation in a way that feels trustworthy. You can check in on what it's doing, you can interrupt it and redirect it, and it asks for confirmation before anything consequential, like making a purchase or sending an email on your behalf.

And over time I'd love for it to feel more personalized, so it knows your preferences, the context of your work, the tools and accounts you use, and you're not re-explaining everything every time. Ultimately the goal is that it feels like delegating to a person you trust, rather than operating a piece of software.

r001.rationale: The response describes checking on, interrupting, and redirecting an agent, but does not propose directly editing the same work the agent is working on.

r002.rationale: It describes asking for work and handing it off, but does not clearly say delegation happens through messages or compare that interaction to messaging a remote coworker.

r003.rationale: It says the user should state what they want and the system should decide whether to search, browse, write code, or answer directly, without the user choosing a tool.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that it should feel like working with a really capable colleague rather than operating a tool. Right now, if you want to use agents, you often have to think about which product does what: this one browses, this one writes code, this one searches your files. The person has to do the routing in their head. What I'd like is for that routing to disappear. You describe what you want, in whatever level of detail you happen to have, and the system figures out which capabilities it needs, whether that's going out to the web, running code, looking at your documents, or taking an action in some app.

The second piece is that it should be asynchronous in a natural way. Some requests take a few seconds, and some take twenty minutes, or run for a week in the background. The interface should handle both without you having to change how you interact. You kick something off, you can go do something else, and it comes back to you with a result, or with a question if it genuinely gets stuck. And that question should be a good one, the kind a thoughtful person would ask, not an interruption every two minutes.

And then trust and visibility. Even if the agent is doing a lot of work, you should be able to see what it did, why it did it, and intervene when you want to. Not a wall of logs, but something closer to a summary a colleague would give you: here's what I looked at, here's what I decided, here's where I wasn't sure. The more capable these systems get, the more that legibility matters, because people will delegate bigger things only if they can check the work when they need to.

So if I had to compress it: one place to ask for anything, it figures out the how, it works on your timescale, and you can always see and steer what it's doing.

r001.rationale: The response says users can see, intervene in, and steer the agent’s work, but does not propose directly editing the same work the agent is editing.

r002.rationale: It proposes describing a request to the system in natural language and compares the experience to working with a capable colleague, which communicates message-like task delegation.

r003.rationale: It says the user should not have to route requests among products and that the system figures out which capabilities are needed.

astra-6.text:
I’d want it to feel like one place where I can hand off work and understand what’s happening without having to manage every step. I can give an agent a task, go do something else, and come back to a result—or a question if it needs something from me.

The interface should make it easy to move between doing something myself and delegating it. Sometimes I want to work closely with the agent, look at what it’s doing, and steer it. Other times I just want it to finish the task and let me know. Those should feel like different levels of involvement in the same workflow, rather than separate products.

r001.rationale: The response describes steering an agent and switching between personal work and delegation, but does not say the person can directly edit the same work the agent is working on.

r002.rationale: It proposes giving an agent a task, but does not specify delegating through messages or frame the interaction as messaging a remote coworker.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose that the interface select which agent handles a task.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want it to feel like one place where I can delegate work, see what’s happening, and step in when I need to. I shouldn’t have to figure out which agent to use or move context between a bunch of different tools. I should be able to describe what I want, have the system ask useful clarifying questions, and then let it get on with the work.

The interesting design challenge is how you move between delegation and collaboration. Sometimes I want to hand something off and come back to a result. Other times I want to work through it together. A unified interface should make that transition feel natural, while keeping it clear what the agents are doing and where they need my input.

r001.rationale: The response describes stepping in and working collaboratively, but does not say the person can directly edit the same work the agent is working on.

r002.rationale: It proposes describing a task to the system, but does not specify delegating through messages or frame the interaction as messaging a remote coworker.

r003.rationale: It says the user should not have to figure out which agent to use, implying the interface selects an agent without requiring the user to choose.
